items.title: The Board
items.content: The game uses a square board of sixty-four squares in an eight-by-eight grid. The squares alternate between a light colour and a dark colour. Every square touches only squares of the other colour along a rank or a file.
items.example: A light square always sits between two dark squares on the same rank.

items.title: Board Orientation
items.content: Each player sets the board so that the square in the near right corner is a light square. A board turned the wrong way puts every diagonal on the wrong colour and moves the king and the queen to the wrong squares.

items.title: Ranks
items.content: A rank is a row of eight squares that runs from one player's left to that player's right. The board holds eight ranks. The ranks carry the numbers 1 to 8, counted from the side that White starts on.
items.example: White's pieces start on rank 1 and Black's pieces start on rank 8.

items.title: Files
items.content: A file is a column of eight squares that runs from one player toward the other. The board holds eight files. The files carry the letters a to h, counted from White's left to White's right.
items.example: The rook in White's near left corner starts on the a file.

items.title: Diagonals
items.content: A diagonal is a line of squares of one colour that touch only at their corners. A diagonal holds from two to eight squares. Every square on one diagonal has the same colour, so a bishop that starts on a light square stays on light squares.

items.title: The Players
items.content: Two players share one board. One player controls the light pieces, called White. The other player controls the dark pieces, called Black. White makes the first move of the game.

items.title: The Pieces
items.content: Each player starts with sixteen pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. A player loses a piece when the opponent captures it, and a captured piece takes no further part in the game.

items.title: The Starting Position
items.content: Each player places the two rooks in the corner squares of their own back rank. A knight stands beside each rook, and a bishop stands beside each knight. The queen and the king take the two squares that remain in the middle. All eight pawns stand on the rank directly in front of the pieces.

items.title: Which Rank Each Side Uses
items.content: White places the pieces on rank 1 and the pawns on rank 2. Black places the pieces on rank 8 and the pawns on rank 7. The four middle ranks start the game empty.

items.title: The Queen Starts on Her Own Colour
items.content: The white queen starts on a light square and the black queen starts on a dark square. The king takes the square beside the queen. This places the two queens on one file and the two kings on the file next to it.
items.example: The white queen starts on d1 and the white king starts on e1.

items.title: Capture
items.content: A square holds one piece at most. When a piece moves to a square that holds an enemy piece, the player takes the enemy piece off the board and puts the moving piece in its place. A player cannot move a piece to a square that holds another of their own pieces. A capture is never compulsory, except when it is the only legal move.
items.example: A rook that travels along an empty file to a square with a black knight removes that knight from the board.

items.title: The Order of Play
items.content: White moves first. After that the players move in turn, and each player makes exactly one move on their turn. A player cannot pass and cannot make two moves in a row. A player must move even when every legal move damages their own position.
items.example: A player whose only legal moves lose material must still choose one of them.

items.title: The Object of the Game
items.content: A player wins by checkmate of the enemy king. A player also wins when the opponent resigns, when the opponent runs out of time, or when the arbiter awards the game. A game that no player wins ends in a draw.

items.title: What a Move Is
items.content: A move takes one piece from the square it stands on to another square. Castling is the single exception, because it moves the king and one rook in the same move. A move to a square with an enemy piece is a capture.

items.title: No Piece Passes Through Another
items.content: A queen, a rook, a bishop, or a pawn stops at the first piece in its path and cannot travel past it. The knight is the only piece that jumps over other pieces.

items.title: A Move Must Not Expose Your Own King
items.content: A player cannot make a move that leaves their own king on a square an enemy piece attacks. A move of that kind is illegal, whether the king was already under attack or the move opens a new line to it.
items.example: A knight that stands between the black king and a white rook on the same file cannot move away.

items.title: The King
items.content: The king moves one square in any direction: along a rank, along a file, or along a diagonal. The king captures on the square it moves to. The king has one further move, which is castling.

items.title: The King Keeps Away From Attacked Squares
items.content: The king cannot move to a square that an enemy piece attacks. This holds even when the enemy piece could not legally make the capture, because that piece stands between its own king and an attacker.

items.title: The Kings Never Touch
items.content: The two kings can never stand on squares that touch. This follows from the rule above, because each king attacks every square beside it.

items.title: The Queen
items.content: The queen moves any number of empty squares along a rank, along a file, or along a diagonal. She stops at the first piece in her path. She captures an enemy piece on that square, and she cannot pass beyond it.
items.example: A queen on d4 on an empty board reaches every square on rank 4, every square on the d file, and every square on the two diagonals through d4.

items.title: The Rook
items.content: The rook moves any number of empty squares along a rank or along a file. It never moves along a diagonal. The rook also takes part in castling, which is a king move.

items.title: The Bishop
items.content: The bishop moves any number of empty squares along a diagonal. A bishop stays on squares of one colour for the whole game, because every diagonal holds squares of one colour only. Each player starts with one light-square bishop and one dark-square bishop.

items.title: The Knight
items.content: The knight moves two squares along a rank or a file, and then one square at a right angle to that direction. The knight jumps over any piece between its start square and its end square. Only the end square matters, and the knight captures an enemy piece there.
items.example: A knight on g1 reaches e2, f3, and h3 from the starting position, although pawns fill the whole of rank 2.

items.title: The Knight Changes Square Colour
items.content: A knight that starts a move on a light square lands on a dark square. A knight that starts a move on a dark square lands on a light square. The colour changes with every knight move.

items.title: The Pawn
items.content: A pawn moves one square straight forward to an empty square. Forward means toward the enemy side of the board. A pawn never moves backward and never moves sideways, so a pawn that passes a square can never come back to it.

items.title: The Two-Square First Move
items.content: A pawn that still stands on its starting rank can move two squares straight forward in one move. Both squares must be empty. A pawn has this option once, and it loses the option after any move.

items.title: How a Pawn Captures
items.content: A pawn captures one square diagonally forward, to the left or to the right. A pawn capture is the only ordinary pawn move that changes the file the pawn stands on. A pawn on a corner file has one capture direction only.
items.example: A white pawn on e4 can capture a black piece on d5 or on f5.

items.title: A Blocked Pawn
items.content: A pawn cannot capture the piece directly in front of it. A piece of either colour on that square stops the pawn from moving forward at all.
items.example: A white pawn on e4 with a black rook on e5 cannot move forward and cannot take that rook. It can still capture on d5 or f5.

items.title: Attacked Squares
items.content: A piece attacks every square it could capture on, whether or not a piece stands there. A pawn attacks only the two squares diagonally in front of it, and not the square it moves to. One piece can attack two or more enemy pieces at the same time, and the defender can then save only one of them.
items.example: A white knight on c7 that attacks a king on a8 and a rook on e8 at the same time wins the rook, because the king must move first.

items.title: An Attack Along a Line
items.content: A queen, a rook, or a bishop attacks along a straight line of squares. When one enemy piece stands on that line and a second enemy piece stands behind it on the same line, the piece in front shields the piece behind. The piece in front cannot leave the line when the piece behind is the king, because that move would be illegal. When the piece behind is worth more, the defender often moves it and gives up the piece in front.
items.example: A white bishop on g5 attacks a black knight on f6 while the black king stands on e7. The knight cannot leave that diagonal.

items.title: An Attack That Opens When a Piece Moves
items.content: A piece that stands between a long-range attacker and an enemy piece opens the line when it moves away. The attack from behind starts at once. The piece that moved can make a threat of its own on the same move, so the opponent faces two threats together.

items.title: Castling
items.content: Castling moves the king two squares toward one of its own rooks along the back rank. In the same move, that rook jumps over the king and lands on the square the king crossed. Castling counts as one move, and a player can castle once in a game at most.

items.title: Short Castling and Long Castling
items.content: Short castling uses the rook nearer to the king, on the h file. Long castling uses the rook further from the king, on the a file. After short castling the king stands on the g file and the rook on the f file. After long castling the king stands on the c file and the rook on the d file.
items.example: White short castling moves the king from e1 to g1 and the rook from h1 to f1.

items.title: The King and Rook Must Not Have Moved
items.content: A player can castle only when the king has made no move in the game and the chosen rook has made no move in the game. A king or a rook that moved away and later returned to its starting square still counts as a piece that moved.

items.title: The Squares Between Must Be Empty
items.content: Every square between the king and the chosen rook must be empty. A piece of either colour on one of those squares stops the move.

items.title: Castling and Check
items.content: A player cannot castle while the king is in check. The king cannot cross a square that an enemy piece attacks, and it cannot land on a square that an enemy piece attacks. The square the rook crosses can be attacked, and the rook itself can be attacked, because neither stops the move.
items.example: A white king on e1 cannot castle short when a black bishop attacks f1. It can castle long when a black rook attacks b1, because the king never stands on b1.

items.title: How to Make the Move
items.content: Castling is a king move. A player who makes the move by hand touches the king first, moves it two squares, and then places the rook.

items.title: The Loss of the Right to Castle
items.content: Once the king moves, the player can never castle again in that game. Once one rook moves, the player can never castle with that rook, although the other rook still allows castling. A player who answers a check with a king move loses the right in the same way.

items.title: En Passant
items.content: A pawn that stands on its fifth rank can capture an enemy pawn that has just moved two squares forward and landed beside it on the same rank. The capture happens as though the enemy pawn had moved one square only. En passant is the one capture in the game that takes a piece from a square the capturing piece does not land on.
items.example: A white pawn stands on e5. Black moves a pawn from d7 to d5. White can answer with a capture on d6, which removes the black pawn from d5.

items.title: The Chance Lasts One Move
items.content: A player can make the capture en passant only as the direct answer to the two-square pawn move. The chance ends as soon as that player makes any other move. It does not come back later.

items.title: Where the Pieces Go
items.content: The capturing pawn lands on the square the enemy pawn crossed. The captured pawn leaves the board from the square it stopped on. Only a pawn can make this capture, and only a pawn can be taken by it.

items.title: Promotion
items.content: A pawn that reaches the far rank of the board must change into a queen, a rook, a bishop, or a knight of the same colour. The player takes the pawn off the board and puts the new piece on the same square. The pawn cannot stay a pawn.

items.title: The Free Choice of Piece
items.content: The player chooses the new piece freely. The choice does not depend on the pieces already captured, so a player can hold two or more queens at the same time. A choice of a rook, a bishop, or a knight is legal, and a player picks one of those to give an immediate check or to keep the opponent out of stalemate.

items.title: The New Piece Acts at Once
items.content: The new piece takes effect the moment it stands on the board. It can give check or checkmate on that same move, and the opponent must answer that check.

items.title: Check
items.content: A king is in check when at least one enemy piece attacks the square it stands on. The player in check must answer the check with their next move. A player does not have to say that they give check, and the opponent must see it.

items.title: The Answers to Check
items.content: A player has three ways to answer a check. They can move the king to a square that no enemy piece attacks. They can capture the checking piece. They can place a piece on a square between the checking piece and the king, which works against a queen, a rook, or a bishop only.
items.example: A check from a knight can be answered by a king move or by a capture of the knight, because no square lies between a knight and the piece it attacks.

items.title: Double Check
items.content: When two enemy pieces attack the king at the same time, only a king move answers the check. No single capture and no single block stops both attacks together.

items.title: An Illegal Answer to Check
items.content: A move that leaves the king in check is illegal. A player who is in check cannot make any move that fails to end the check, and cannot castle.

items.title: Checkmate
items.content: A player is checkmated when their king is in check and they have no legal move. The game ends at that moment, and the player who gave the checkmate wins. No later move is played.
items.example: A black king on h8 faces a white queen on g7 that a white bishop on b2 defends. The king cannot take the queen and cannot move to g8 or h7, so the position is checkmate.

items.title: The King Is Never Captured
items.content: No player ever captures a king. The game ends at checkmate, one move before a capture of the king could happen. A king therefore never leaves the board.

items.title: Stalemate
items.content: A player is stalemated when they have no legal move and their king is not in check. The game ends at that moment in a draw. Stalemate and checkmate differ in one point only: the king is under attack in checkmate and safe in stalemate.
items.example: A black king alone on a8, with a white king on c7 and a white queen on b6, has no legal move and stands on a square no piece attacks. The game is a draw.

items.title: A Draw by Agreement
items.content: The two players can agree to a draw. One player makes a move, offers the draw, and then presses the clock. The offer stands until the opponent accepts it, declines it in words, or makes a move. A move by the opponent declines the offer.

items.title: Threefold Repetition
items.content: A player can claim a draw when the same position appears on the board three times, with the same player to move each time. The three appearances do not have to follow one after the other. The player claims the draw before making the move that would produce the third appearance, or when the third appearance already stands on the board.

items.title: When Two Positions Are the Same
items.content: Two positions count as the same only when four things match. Every piece of the same kind and colour stands on the same square. The same player has the move. The castling rights are equal. The same capture en passant is available in both. A change in any of these makes a different position.

items.title: Fivefold Repetition
items.content: When the same position appears five times, the game is a draw. Neither player has to claim it, and the arbiter can declare the result.

items.title: The Fifty-Move Rule
items.content: A player can claim a draw when each player has made fifty moves in a row with no capture and no pawn move. Any capture resets the count to zero, and any pawn move resets the count to zero. The scoresheet is the proof of the count.

items.title: The Seventy-Five-Move Rule
items.content: When each player has made seventy-five moves in a row with no capture and no pawn move, the game is a draw without a claim. A move that gives checkmate ends the game as a win instead.

items.title: A Dead Position
items.content: A position is dead when no series of legal moves can produce a checkmate for either player. The game is a draw at that moment. King against king is dead. King and bishop against king is dead, and so is king and knight against king. King and bishop against king and bishop is dead when both bishops travel on squares of the same colour.
items.example: Two bare kings on the board can never produce a checkmate, so the game is a draw as soon as the last other piece leaves.

items.title: Perpetual Check
items.content: A player can sometimes give check on every move and leave the opponent no way out of the sequence. This is not a separate way to end a game. The game ends as a draw through the repetition of the position or through the fifty-move count, and a player who wants the draw claims it under one of those rules.

items.title: The Chess Clock
items.content: A chess clock holds two displays in one housing. Only one display runs at a time, and it belongs to the player who has the move. The time control states how much time each player receives for the game or for a set number of moves.

items.title: Pressing the Clock
items.content: A player completes a move and then presses the clock, which stops their own time and starts the opponent's time. The player moves the piece and presses the clock with the same hand. A player who does not press the clock keeps losing their own time.

items.title: The Fall of the Flag
items.content: The fall of the flag is the moment a player's time reaches zero. That player loses the game, as long as the opponent or the arbiter points it out. A player who notices their own flag has fallen can also state it.

items.title: A Flag Fall With Too Little Material
items.content: A player whose time runs out does not lose when the opponent has no series of legal moves that could produce a checkmate. The game is a draw in that case.
items.example: A player with a lone king cannot win on time, because a lone king can never give checkmate.

items.title: Increment and Delay
items.content: An increment adds a fixed amount of time to a player's clock after every move that player makes. A delay holds the clock still for a fixed amount of time before the player's own time starts to fall. A time control can use one of these, or neither.
items.example: A control of ten minutes with a five-second increment gives each player five more seconds after each of their moves.

items.title: Algebraic Notation
items.content: Algebraic notation names every square with one letter and one number. The letter names the file, from a to h. The number names the rank, from 1 to 8. The square in White's near left corner is a1, and the square in Black's near left corner is h8.
items.example: The four middle squares of the board are d4, e4, d5, and e5.

items.title: The Letters for the Pieces
items.content: A move record writes K for the king, Q for the queen, R for the rook, B for the bishop, and N for the knight. A pawn move carries no letter and shows the end square alone.
items.example: Nf3 records a knight move to f3. e4 records a pawn move to e4.

items.title: How to Write a Capture
items.content: A capture takes the sign x between the piece letter and the end square. A pawn capture names the file the pawn left, then x, then the end square. A capture en passant is written like any other pawn capture, and some records add the letters e.p. after it.
items.example: Bxc6 records a bishop that captures on c6. exd5 records a pawn from the e file that captures on d5.

items.title: The Signs for Check and Checkmate
items.content: A move that gives check takes a plus sign at the end of the record. A move that gives checkmate takes a hash sign at the end of the record.
items.example: Qh5+ gives check. Qxf7# gives checkmate.

items.title: How to Write Castling
items.content: Short castling is written O-O. Long castling is written O-O-O. The character is the capital letter O, and not the digit zero.

items.title: How to Write a Promotion
items.content: A promotion writes the pawn move, then an equals sign, then the letter of the new piece.
items.example: e8=Q records a pawn that reaches e8 and becomes a queen. exd8=N+ records a pawn capture on d8 that becomes a knight and gives check.

items.title: Two Pieces Can Reach the Same Square
items.content: When two pieces of the same kind can move to the same square, the record adds the file the piece came from. When both pieces stand on one file, the record adds the rank instead. When neither is enough, the record adds the file and the rank.
items.example: Nbd2 names the knight that came from the b file. R1a3 names the rook that came from rank 1.

items.title: Move Numbers and the Scoresheet
items.content: Each player writes both moves of every turn on a scoresheet as the game goes on, in a clear and readable form. A number marks each turn, and White's move comes before Black's move. The scoresheet is the record that a claim for a draw rests on, and the arbiter reads it to settle a dispute.
items.example: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 records the first two turns of a game.

items.title: Touch-Move
items.content: A player who touches one of their own pieces on purpose must move that piece, when that piece has a legal move. The obligation starts at the moment of the touch, and the player cannot then choose a different piece. When the touched piece has no legal move, the player moves any piece they wish.

items.title: Touching an Enemy Piece
items.content: A player who touches an enemy piece on purpose must capture it, when a legal capture of that piece exists. When no legal capture exists, the touch carries no obligation.

items.title: The Words That Allow an Adjustment
items.content: A player who wants to place a piece neatly in the centre of its square says so before the touch. The player must have the move at that time. After the announcement the touch carries no obligation, and the player can then move any piece.

items.title: When a Move Is Complete
items.content: A move is complete when the player's hand releases the piece on a legal square. A capture is complete when the hand releases the capturing piece, after the captured piece has left the board. A complete move cannot be taken back.

items.title: Touch-Move and Castling
items.content: A player who touches the king first can still castle, because castling is a king move. A player who touches a rook first must move that rook alone, and cannot castle on that move.

items.title: An Illegal Move
items.content: An illegal move stands corrected as soon as either player notices it. The players restore the position from before the move, and the player then makes a legal move with the piece they touched, when such a move exists. A player who makes more than one illegal move in the same game can lose the game, at the arbiter's decision.

items.title: Help and Distraction Are Forbidden
items.content: A player cannot use notes, advice from another person, or a computer during a game. A player cannot distract or disturb the opponent in any way. A draw offer that a player repeats after a refusal counts as a disturbance.

items.title: The Arbiter
items.content: The arbiter watches the games, applies these rules, and settles any dispute. A player who wants a ruling stops the clock and calls the arbiter. The arbiter's decision holds for that game.

items.title: Resignation
items.content: A player can resign at any point and lose the game at that moment. A player resigns by saying so plainly, by stopping the clock and stating it, or by writing the result on the scoresheet. A resignation cannot be withdrawn.

items.title: The Score of a Game
items.content: A win scores one point and a loss scores no point. A draw scores half a point for each player. The result is written 1-0 for a win by White, 0-1 for a win by Black, and 1/2-1/2 for a draw.
